subject: anti-reflective optical coating
object: less reflection can improve transmission and image contrast while performance changes with wavelength and incident angle
quotes: An anti-reflective ( AR ), anti-glare or anti-reflection coating is a type of optical coating applied to the surface of lenses , other optical elements, and photovoltaic cells to reduce reflection .
This makes the structure's performance change with wavelength and incident angle , so that color effects often appear at oblique angles .
accepted: Anti-reflective coatings can reduce reflection and stray light, improving transmission and contrast, while performance depends on wavelength and angle. The mechanism does not establish which exact seller lens has the best coating or a visible output advantage.

subject: prime lens category
object: a prime is less versatile than a zoom and is often, but not automatically, faster, lighter or optically superior
quotes: In film and photography, a prime lens is a fixed focal length photographic lens (as opposed to a zoom lens ), typically with a maximum aperture from f2.8 to f1.2.
While a prime lens of a given focal length is less versatile than a zoom lens, it is often of superior optical quality, wider maximum aperture, lighter weight, and smaller size.
accepted: A photographic prime is a fixed-focal-length lens; compared with a zoom it is less versatile and is often faster, lighter, smaller or optically better. Often is not always, and the category statement does not rank the exact 35mm, 40mm, 50mm and zoom offers.

subject: Canon EF-S 18-55mm lens family
object: the family covers a 28.8-88mm equivalent field of view and includes a basic III iteration among several distinct versions
quotes: it is a standard kit lens on Canon's consumer APS-C DSLRs.

subject: Canon EF 50mm lens on APS-C
object: the crop factor yields an approximately 80mm field of view on a Canon APS-C DSLR
quotes: When pairing a 50mm lens to a Canon DSLR with an APS-C sized sensor, the crop factor effectively turns the 50mm focal length into an 80mm field of view.
accepted: A Canon EF 50mm lens on an APS-C DSLR gives roughly an 80mm-equivalent field of view. That may suit portraits but can be restrictive indoors; it is format context, not proof of task fit or superior output.

subject: photographic lens design
object: light capture, color, evenness, sharpness, flare, aberrations, weight, cost and mechanical operation are traded against sensor and use limits
quotes: The design of photographic lenses for use in still or cine cameras is intended to produce a lens that yields the most acceptable rendition of the subject being photographed within a range of constraints that include cost, weight and materials.
photographic lenses are not always designed for maximum possible resolution since the recording medium would not be able to record the level of detail that the lens could resolve.
accepted: Photographic lens design balances acceptable rendition against cost, weight, materials, flare, aberrations and mechanical behavior, and maximum possible resolution may exceed the recording medium's needs. This rejects a one-dimensional price-to-sharpness cutoff.

subject: chromatic aberration
object: dispersion can produce color fringes, with axial and transverse forms behaving differently
quotes: In optics , chromatic aberration ( CA ), also called chromatic distortion , color aberration , color fringing , or purple fringing , is a failure of a lens to focus all colors to the same point.
Chromatic aberration manifests itself as "fringes" of color along boundaries that separate dark and bright parts of the image.
accepted: Chromatic aberration occurs when colors do not share one focus or magnification and can appear as colored fringes at contrast boundaries. It must be measured by position, aperture and output rather than inferred from price or a product label.

subject: spherical aberration
object: the effect can be stronger at short focal ratios and can be corrected with optical design choices
quotes: Light rays that strike a spherical surface off-centre are refracted or reflected more or less than those that strike close to the centre. This deviation reduces the quality of images produced by optical systems.

The effect is proportional to the fourth power of the diameter and inversely proportional to the third power of the focal length, so it is much more pronounced at short focal ratios , i.e., "fast" lenses.
accepted: Spherical aberration can make central and outer rays focus differently and may be more pronounced at fast focal ratios, while design can correct it. A wider f-number alone therefore neither guarantees nor disproves sharp output.

subject: vignetting
object: it can arise from lens, settings, filters or hoods and can also be used intentionally
quotes: vignetting ( / v Éª n Ë j É t Éª Å / vin- YET -ing ) is a reduction of an image's brightness or saturation toward the periphery compared to the image center.
Vignetting is often an unintended and undesired effect caused by camera settings or lens limitations.  However, it is sometimes deliberately introduced for creative effect
accepted: Vignetting is peripheral brightness or saturation reduction and may come from settings, lens limitations, filters or hoods; it can also be intentional. It needs frame-position, aperture and accessory tests rather than a universal pass or fail.

subject: lens flare
object: bright sources, optical interfaces and shading affect visible artifacts and contrast loss
quotes: A lens flare is a visual artifact caused by light scattering , or flaring, in a lens system.
The glare makes the image look "washed out" by reducing contrast and color saturation
accepted: Lens flare comes from scattering or internal reflection and can create visible artifacts or washed-out contrast, especially with bright sources. It must be tested with declared light position and hood use, not inferred from element count, coating copy or price.

subject: optical transfer function
object: contrast transfer varies with spatial frequency, focus and the full imaging chain
quotes: The optical transfer function ( OTF ) of an optical system such as a camera , microscope , human eye , or projector is a scale-dependent description of their imaging contrast.
This derived function is commonly referred to as the modulation transfer function ( MTF ).
accepted: OTF, and its commonly used magnitude MTF, describes how imaging contrast changes with spatial scale. It is not one context-free sharpness score and must be tied to focus, sensor, processing, display or print size and relevant detail.

subject: diffraction limit
object: smaller apertures increase diffraction and at f/22 many modern lenses can be diffraction limited
quotes: any optical instrument or system â a microscope , telescope , or camera â has a principal limit to its resolution due to the physics of diffraction .
At small apertures, such as f/22 , most modern lenses are limited only by diffraction and not by aberrations or other imperfections in the construction.
accepted: Diffraction sets a physical resolution limit and grows as the aperture is made smaller; at f/22 many modern lenses can be diffraction limited. Stopping down can reduce some aberrations yet eventually reduce detail, so aperture tests need the intended output.
